stem: A 52-year-old man is found confused and vomiting in a closed room heated by a faulty gas heater in winter. He has a headache and flushed pink skin. The pulse oximeter reads 98% and arterial PaO2 is 95 mm Hg. Co-oximetry is then performed.
oneliner: 52M + confusion + headache + closed room with faulty heater + pink skin + pulse oximetry 98% + PaO2 95 → which set of O2 values and curve shift?
ask: Which set of changes best fits his true oxygen status?

options.A: PaO2 ↓, O2 saturation ↓, O2 content ↓, curve shift right
options.B: PaO2 ↔, O2 saturation ↔, O2 content ↓, curve shift none
options.C: PaO2 ↔, O2 saturation ↓, O2 content ↓, curve shift right
options.D: PaO2 ↔, O2 saturation ↓, O2 content ↓, curve shift left
options.E: PaO2 ↓, O2 saturation ↓, O2 content ↓, curve shift left

whyNot.A: Low PaO2 is simple hypoxemia; his PaO2 is **95**, and the abnormal binding **shifts the curve left**
whyNot.B: Normal saturation with low content fits **too little hemoglobin**; a faulty gas heater points to a gas that occupies hemoglobin and lowers true saturation
whyNot.C: Right is wrong: bound CO makes remaining hemoglobin **hold oxygen more tightly**, so the curve moves left
whyNot.E: The left shift is right but PaO2 is **not** reduced; CO does not lower oxygen dissolved in plasma

answer: Normal PaO2, low saturation and content, left-shifted curve
why: **Carbon monoxide** binds hemoglobin with about 200-fold higher affinity than oxygen. It occupies sites, so **true saturation and content fall** while dissolved oxygen, **PaO2, stays normal**. It also increases the affinity of the remaining sites, a **left shift**. Standard pulse oximetry misreads carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin.
chain: Fewer sites for oxygen: saturation and content fall
PaO2 unchanged because the lungs transfer oxygen normally
Remaining sites hold oxygen tighter: curve shifts left (P50 down)

idea.rule: CO: PaO2 normal, saturation and content down, curve left.
also: Methemoglobinemia (nitrites, dapsone): PaO2 normal, saturation and content down, curve left
Methylene chloride (paint stripper) is metabolized to CO
Standard pulse oximetry reads falsely normal in CO poisoning

stem: A 58-year-old man in the ICU receives a drug by constant IV infusion at 100 mg/h. After several days his plasma concentration has stopped changing and measures 50 mg/L.
oneliner: 58M + constant IV infusion 100 mg/h + plasma level plateau 50 mg/L → clearance?
ask: What is this drug's clearance in him?

whyNot.A: That is 50 ÷ 100, the **ratio turned upside down**; clearance is rate ÷ concentration (100 ÷ 50)
whyNot.B: At 50 L/h the same 100 mg/h would give a level of only **2 mg/L** (100 ÷ 50), not 50 mg/L
whyNot.D: That is 100 × 50, a **product**; and mg/h is a rate of elimination, not a clearance (L/h)
whyNot.E: The number is right but the **unit** is wrong: clearance is volume of plasma cleared per hour, not mg/h

why: At steady state **rate in = rate out**, and rate out = CL × Css. So CL = 100 mg/h ÷ 50 mg/L = **2 L/h**. Check: 2 L/h × 50 mg/L = 100 mg/h, matching the infusion.
chain: Level rises until elimination matches input, then plateaus
If CL were lower, the same infusion would settle at a higher Css

idea.rule: At steady state, clearance = infusion rate ÷ steady-state concentration.
also: Maintenance dose = CL × target Css (÷ F if oral)
Doubling the infusion rate doubles Css for a first-order drug
Time to steady state is about 4 to 5 half-lives, whatever the dose

stem: An 80-year-old man is given a single 80 mg IV bolus of a drug. Once distribution is complete, the plasma level is 4 micrograms/mL. The distribution half-life is 3 minutes and the elimination half-life is 24 hours.
oneliner: 80M + 80 mg IV bolus + level 4 micrograms/mL after distribution → volume of distribution?
ask: What is the drug's apparent volume of distribution?

whyNot.A: Would need a level of **40 mg/L** (80 ÷ 2); his level is 4 mg/L
whyNot.B: Would need a level of **16 mg/L** (80 ÷ 5), not 4 mg/L
whyNot.C: Would need a level of **8 mg/L** (80 ÷ 10), double the measured 4 mg/L
whyNot.E: Would give only **1.6 mg/L** (80 ÷ 50), well under the measured 4 mg/L

why: Vd = dose ÷ initial concentration = 80 mg ÷ 4 mg/L = **20 L** (4 micrograms/mL is the same as 4 mg/L). The half-lives only show that distribution is over in minutes while **almost none of the drug has been eliminated**, so they do not change the calculation.
chain: Drug spreads into tissues until the level settles at 4 mg/L
Vd is the volume that would hold 80 mg at 4 mg/L
A bigger Vd would leave the same dose at a lower level

shifts.var: Plasma level if Vd is larger

idea.rule: Vd = amount of drug in the body ÷ plasma concentration.
also: Lipophilic drugs have a large Vd; highly protein-bound drugs a small one
For the same dose, a larger Vd gives a lower plasma level

stem: A 70-year-old man with a creatinine clearance of 25 mL/min is starting IV vancomycin. The team wants the same target plasma concentration used in patients with normal kidney function.
oneliner: 70M + creatinine clearance 25 mL/min + IV vancomycin + same target concentration → which value differs?
ask: Which of the following will differ from the values used in a patient with normal kidney function?

whyNot.B: Loading dose = Vd × target concentration, and **neither is changed** by lower GFR, so it stays the same
whyNot.C: Vd is a property of how the drug distributes; **GFR does not alter it**
whyNot.D: The drug is given **IV**, so bioavailability is 100% whatever the kidneys do
whyNot.E: The team has chosen **the same target**; the dose is changed to reach it

why: Vancomycin is cleared by the kidney, so low GFR **lowers clearance**. Maintenance dose = CL × target Css, so the **maintenance dose must fall**; half-life and time to steady state lengthen, but the **loading dose (Vd × target) is unchanged**.
chain: Half-life (0.7 × Vd ÷ CL) lengthens, so steady state takes longer
Maintenance dose = CL × target Css must fall
Loading dose = Vd × target is unaffected

idea.rule: Falling GFR lowers clearance of renally cleared drugs: cut the maintenance dose, keep the loading dose.

stem: A 45-year-old obese man and a lean man of the same age are each given the same fixed IV dose of a highly lipophilic drug. In the obese man, the plasma concentration is lower and the half-life is longer than in the lean man.
oneliner: 45M obese + same IV dose of lipophilic drug as a lean man + lower plasma level + longer half-life → which property?
ask: Which pharmacokinetic property best explains this?

whyNot.A: Higher clearance would **shorten** the half-life; his is longer
whyNot.B: The dose is given **IV**, so bioavailability is already 100%
whyNot.C: More binding in plasma would keep drug in plasma and lower Vd, giving a **higher** plasma level, not a lower one
whyNot.D: Faster metabolism is higher clearance, which again would **shorten** the half-life

why: A lipophilic drug spreads into excess body fat, so Vd is **larger**. The same dose is diluted into a bigger volume, so the **plasma level falls**; and since t1/2 = 0.7 × Vd ÷ CL, with clearance unchanged the **half-life lengthens**.
chain: Same dose in a larger volume gives a lower plasma concentration
t1/2 = 0.7 × Vd ÷ CL, so half-life rises

idea.rule: Larger Vd means lower plasma level and longer half-life if clearance is unchanged.
also: Lipophilic drugs accumulate in fat in obesity
Edema and ascites enlarge Vd of hydrophilic drugs
Dehydration and a low-fat body shrink Vd

stem: Healthy volunteers are given enough ethanol to reach blood levels of 150 mg/dL in one group and 300 mg/dL in another. Serial sampling shows that blood ethanol falls by about 15 mg/dL every hour in both groups, whatever the starting level.
oneliner: Blood ethanol 150 vs 300 mg/dL + same fall of ~15 mg/dL every hour in both → which elimination kinetics?
ask: Which type of elimination does this show?

whyNot.A: First-order removes a **constant fraction** per hour, so the 300 group would fall twice as fast in absolute terms
whyNot.C: Distribution between compartments gives a **fast early drop** then a slower one, not a steady linear fall
whyNot.D: Recirculation would produce a **secondary rise**, not a steady linear fall
whyNot.E: Flow-limited clearance is for drugs extracted by the liver so fast that **blood flow** limits removal, giving first-order decay

why: At concentrations far above Km the **enzymes are saturated**, so removal runs at **Vmax: a constant amount per hour** regardless of concentration. A small dose increase therefore causes a disproportionate rise in level, and half-life lengthens as the level rises.
chain: Same mg per hour whatever the level
Higher levels take proportionally longer to clear

shifts.var: Fraction eliminated per hour at the higher level
Apparent half-life at the higher level

idea.rule: Saturated enzymes = zero-order: a constant amount, not a constant fraction, is eliminated per unit time.
also: Small dose increases cause large level rises

stem: A 50-year-old man with epilepsy has been stable on phenytoin for years with no dose change. Two weeks after a drug for duodenal ulcer is added, he develops nystagmus, ataxia and slurred speech. His phenytoin concentration has doubled.
oneliner: 50M + epilepsy stable on phenytoin + new ulcer drug + nystagmus, ataxia + phenytoin level doubled → which drug?
ask: Which newly added drug most likely caused this?

whyNot.B: An H2 blocker that **does not inhibit CYP450**, so the phenytoin level would not double
whyNot.C: An H2 blocker **without CYP450 inhibition**; phenytoin clearance would be unchanged
whyNot.D: Sucralfate stays in the gut and can **reduce phenytoin absorption**, which would lower the level, not double it
whyNot.E: A prostaglandin E1 analog that **does not inhibit CYP450**, so it would not raise the phenytoin level

why: Cimetidine is a **CYP450 inhibitor**, so phenytoin clearance falls and its level rises to toxicity (nystagmus, ataxia). **Ranitidine and famotidine** are also H2 blockers but do **not** inhibit CYP450.

idea.rule: CYP450 inhibitors lower clearance, raising levels of the substrate drug.

stem: A 49-year-old man who has drunk heavily every day for ten years needs 10 mg of warfarin daily when sober, double the usual dose. After a weekend binge his INR rises to 6.0 on the same dose.
oneliner: 49M + daily heavy drinking for 10 years + needs double warfarin dose sober + INR rises after a binge → what changes?
ask: Which change in drug metabolism best explains both observations?

options.A: Chronic induction of glucuronidation; no acute change
options.B: Higher plasma protein binding when sober, lower during a binge
options.C: Chronic CYP450 induction; acute CYP450 inhibition
options.D: Greater renal excretion when sober, lower during a binge
options.E: Smaller volume of distribution after a binge, unchanged when sober

whyNot.A: Cannot explain the **INR rise during the binge**; it gives no acute effect
whyNot.B: A change in binding would not give **opposite effects** in the sober and binge states
whyNot.D: Nothing points to a renal change; the shift is in **liver metabolism** between the two states
whyNot.E: A volume change would not explain the **higher dose needed when sober**

answer: Chronic induction of CYP450 and acute inhibition
why: Chronic heavy drinking **induces CYP450**, so warfarin is cleared faster and a larger dose is needed. A binge **competes for and inhibits CYP450**, so clearance falls and the same dose now gives a high INR.
chain: Warfarin clearance rises, so a higher dose is needed
Clearance drops on the same dose

idea.rule: Chronic alcohol induces CYP450; acute alcohol inhibits it.
also: Warfarin, phenytoin and diazepam levels follow the same pattern
Other inducers: rifampin, carbamazepine, barbiturates, St John's wort

stem: In an isolated tissue experiment, three agonists X, Y and Z act on the same receptor. The concentration giving half of each drug's own maximal response is 1 nM for X, 10 nM for Y and 100 nM for Z. Maximal response is 60% of the tissue maximum for X and 100% for both Y and Z.
oneliner: Three agonists + half-maximal at 1, 10, 100 nM + plateau 60%, 100%, 100% → most potent?
ask: Which drug is the most potent?

options.D: Y and Z equally, X less

whyNot.A: Y needs **10 nM** for half-maximal effect, ten times more than X; its full plateau is **efficacy**, not potency
whyNot.B: Z needs the **highest concentration (100 nM)**, so it is the least potent
whyNot.C: They need very different concentrations (**1, 10 and 100 nM**) for half-maximal effect
whyNot.D: That ranks the drugs by **plateau height**, which is efficacy, not potency

why: Potency is read on the **concentration axis**: X reaches 50% of its effect at the **lowest EC50 (1 nM)**, so it is most potent. Its plateau is lower (60%), so it is **less efficacious**: potency and efficacy are independent.
chain: Compare concentration needed for half-maximal effect
X needs 1 nM, Y 10 nM, Z 100 nM
X plateaus at 60%, so it is less efficacious

shifts.var: EC50 of X (vs Y and Z)

idea.rule: Potency = position along the x-axis (lowest EC50); efficacy = height of the plateau (Emax).
also: Competitive antagonists shift the curve right without changing Emax

stem: A table lists four inhaled anesthetics. Blood:gas, oil:gas and MAC: nitrous oxide 0.47, 1.4, 104%; desflurane 0.45, 19, 6.0%; sevoflurane 0.65, 47, 2.0%; halothane 2.3, 224, 0.75%.
oneliner: Table of four inhaled anesthetics with blood:gas, oil:gas and MAC → which property tracks potency?
ask: Which property best predicts an agent's potency?

whyNot.A: The two lowest values (**0.47 and 0.45**) belong to the two **least** potent agents; low blood solubility gives **fast onset**, not potency
whyNot.C: A **high MAC** (nitrous oxide, 104%) means a large concentration is needed, so it marks **low** potency
whyNot.D: Desflurane (**0.45**) is far more potent than nitrous oxide (**0.47**) despite similar blood:gas values, so blood:gas does not track potency
whyNot.E: **Molecular weight is not in the table** and does not set potency

why: Potency rises with lipid solubility: **halothane has the highest oil:gas (224) and the lowest MAC (0.75%)**, nitrous oxide the reverse. Speed of onset is different; it follows **low blood solubility**.
chain: Higher oil:gas goes with lower MAC
Blood:gas does not follow the same order

idea.rule: Potency = lipid solubility (high oil:gas, low MAC); speed of onset = low blood:gas.
also: Nitrous oxide: low potency, fast onset

stem: A 38-year-old man is breathing a fixed concentration of a volatile anesthetic by mask, and induction is slow.
oneliner: 38M + fixed inspired concentration of volatile anesthetic by mask + slow induction → which change speeds it most?
ask: Which combination would speed up induction the most?

options.A: Higher minute ventilation, higher cardiac output
options.B: Lower minute ventilation, lower cardiac output
options.C: Lower minute ventilation, higher cardiac output
options.D: Higher minute ventilation, lower cardiac output
options.E: No change in minute ventilation or cardiac output

whyNot.A: More agent is delivered, but a **higher cardiac output** carries it away in blood, so the net gain is blunted
whyNot.B: **Less delivery** to the alveoli slows the rise; the lower cardiac output cannot fully offset it
whyNot.C: **Less delivery plus more uptake** make induction slowest
whyNot.E: Without any change, induction **stays slow**, as in the current picture

answer: Higher minute ventilation with lower cardiac output
why: Induction is faster when the alveolar partial pressure rises quickly. **Higher ventilation delivers more agent**, and **lower cardiac output means less agent is removed by blood**, so the alveolar concentration approaches the inspired one sooner.
chain: Ventilation rises, so more agent reaches the alveoli
Cardiac output falls, so less is carried off in blood

shifts.var: Rate of rise of alveolar anesthetic

idea.rule: Fast induction = more delivery (high ventilation) and less uptake (low cardiac output, low blood solubility).
also: Low blood:gas agents (nitrous oxide, desflurane) reach equilibrium fastest

stem: A 30-year-old man had apnea lasting three hours after succinylcholine for a first operation; plasma cholinesterase activity was found to be very low. He now needs a second operation and an alternative muscle relaxant is considered.
oneliner: 30M + prolonged apnea after succinylcholine + low plasma cholinesterase + needs another relaxant → which would also be prolonged?
ask: Which drug will also have a prolonged effect?

whyNot.A: An aminosteroid cleared by **liver and bile**, not by plasma cholinesterase
whyNot.B: An aminosteroid cleared by the **liver**, not by plasma cholinesterase
whyNot.C: Broken down spontaneously by **Hofmann elimination**, independent of the enzyme
whyNot.D: An aminosteroid cleared mainly by the **kidney**, not by plasma cholinesterase

why: Succinylcholine is hydrolyzed by **plasma cholinesterase**, so a deficiency prolongs it. **Mivacurium** is cleared the same way, so its block also lasts longer. The other agents are cleared by other routes.
chain: Ester-type drugs are broken down slowly

idea.rule: Drugs inactivated by plasma cholinesterase last longer when it is deficient.
also: Ester local anesthetics such as chloroprocaine and procaine

stem: A 34-year-old woman is brought in with headache and nausea along with the rest of her family; the household heater flue is found cracked. Her carboxyhemoglobin is 28%, and its half-life on room air is 4 to 5 hours. She is given 100% oxygen through a tight-fitting mask at normal atmospheric pressure.
oneliner: 34F + headache, nausea, family affected, cracked heater flue + COHb 28% + 100% oxygen by mask → half-life now?
ask: What is the approximate carboxyhemoglobin half-life during this treatment?

whyNot.B: Oxygen **competes** with CO for hemoglobin, so the half-life does not stay the same
whyNot.C: Oxygen would **shorten** the half-life, not lengthen it
whyNot.D: CO dissociates from hemoglobin **slowly**; minutes is far too fast
whyNot.E: That fits **hyperbaric** oxygen; she was treated at **atmospheric pressure**

why: CO binds hemoglobin about 200 times more tightly than oxygen, so on room air it clears with a half-life of **4 to 5 hours**. High-flow **100% oxygen at atmospheric pressure** cuts this to about **1 hour**, and hyperbaric oxygen shortens it further.

idea.rule: High-dose oxygen competes CO off hemoglobin: half-life falls from about 4 to 5 hours to about 1 hour.
also: Hyperbaric oxygen shortens it to about 20 to 30 minutes
Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal in CO poisoning
Cherry-red skin is a late and unreliable sign

stem: A 27-year-old man has been drinking heavily and eating nothing for three days. He is found confused with a glucose of 30 mg/dL.
oneliner: 27M + heavy drinking, no food for 3 days + confusion + glucose 30 mg/dL → which hepatic change explains it?
ask: Which change in the liver most directly causes the low glucose?

whyNot.A: Acetyl-CoA actually **activates pyruvate carboxylase**, which would favour glucose production
whyNot.B: ATP is **not the block**; the problem is in the redox state
whyNot.D: Oxaloacetate **falls**, because it is diverted to malate
whyNot.E: PEP **falls**, because the pathway is blocked upstream of it

why: Ethanol oxidation generates large amounts of **NADH**. The high NADH/NAD+ ratio pushes pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, so **gluconeogenesis is blocked**. With glycogen exhausted after fasting, glucose falls.
chain: Ethanol is oxidized to acetaldehyde and acetate
Pyruvate diverted to lactate, oxaloacetate to malate
Glycogen already used, so glucose falls

idea.rule: Ethanol metabolism raises NADH/NAD+, blocking gluconeogenesis; after fasting glycogen is gone, so hypoglycemia follows.
also: Lactic acidosis from pyruvate to lactate
Fatty liver from fatty acid synthesis
Hyperuricemia from lactate competing with urate excretion
